strengths: Scale and annotation breadth are genuinely substantial: 21,789 hours of raw in-the-wild video distilled into 7,089 hours / 2.7M clips with per-frame camera poses, depth maps, dynamic masks, structured captions, and serialized motion instructions. Table 1 shows SpatialVID dominating prior spatial datasets (CO3Dv2, RealEstate10K, DL3DV, Waymo, Panda-70M, etc.) in both scale and annotation richness, which is a real contribution to the community if the data is released.

The curation pipeline is thorough and well documented: motion-first manual screening, hierarchical multi-criteria filtering (aesthetics via CLIP+MLP, luminance, OCR text-area, motion via VMAF), modified PySceneDetect segmentation for fades, and a two-stage sampling procedure that produces a class-balanced HQ subset (Fig. 2, 3, 5, 10).

The structured-caption design that injects camera poses as a geometric prior into the LLM refinement stage is a sensible and well-motivated idea. Figure 9 gives a convincing qualitative example where the VLM mislabels a left pan as right and the pose-conditioned refinement corrects it — a concrete failure mode of pure VLM captioning that this dataset explicitly addresses.

Motion-instruction decomposition into a standardized cinematic vocabulary (dolly in, pan left, truck right, etc., Fig. 7) derived from pose deltas is directly consumable by controllable video generation / world-model training, and the inclusion of MoveDist, RotAngle, and TrajTurns as quantitative motion descriptors is a useful, reusable evaluation formalism.

Reasonable empirical grounding for design choices: Fig. 6 compares MegaSaM against COLMAP, DROID-SLAM, Fast3R, MonST3R and VGGT with trajectory visualizations, and Sec. 4.3 compares quality/motion distributions against Panda-70M.
weaknesses: No downstream experiments of any kind. The abstract claims the data statistics "directly foster improved model generalization and performance," but the paper contains no training or evaluation on any task (camera pose estimation, depth prediction, controllable video generation, navigation, embodied agents). For a dataset paper, this is the central missing piece: the utility claim is asserted, not demonstrated. At minimum, a controlled comparison (e.g., fine-tuning a pose estimator or a camera-controlled video generator on SpatialVID vs. a baseline corpus) is needed.

The annotations are pseudo-labels produced by off-the-shelf models (MegaSaM with UniDepth v2 / Depth Anything v2, SAM2, Gemini-2.0-flash, Qwen3-30B) and are never quantitatively validated. There is no comparison of the estimated poses/depths against any sequence with real ground truth, no reprojection-error or trajectory-error statistics, and no assessment of dynamic-mask quality or caption hallucination. The abstract's phrasing "ground-truth camera motion" is misleading for SLAM-derived poses; the paper even notes MegaSaM fails when objects dominate the view or motion is collinear, so error propagation into the labels is a real concern that goes unquantified.

The comparison with Panda-70M (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 13) is circular: the same metrics used as SpatialVID's filtering criteria (aesthetics, luminance, motion) are then used to show that SpatialVID scores better on those metrics. This is close to tautological and does not establish that the dataset is more useful for learning. The TrajTurns analysis ("over 80% of Panda-70M videos cannot be reconstructed by MegaSaM") also measures MegaSaM's failure rather than the source data's properties.

Ethical, legal, and licensing aspects of a 33,443-video YouTube crawl are entirely unaddressed: no discussion of terms of service, copyright status of redistributed content, privacy/PII (faces, license plates, captions mentioning people), or the annotation-license terms under which the dataset will be released. Reproducibility also suffers because the paper gives no dataset release URL, license, or split definition, and no benchmark task/protocol is defined for future users.

The "largest" and "surpassing current datasets" claims are supported by Table 1, but that table mixes incommensurable units (hours, Scenes, Clips, Frames, ~1.19M vs. 127.60M) without normalizing, and several competing entries are concurrent works (e.g., Sekai) whose final numbers may not be comparable. The claim of being the largest dynamic video dataset with explicit geometric annotations is thus only loosely established.

Several design decisions are justified only qualitatively. The choice of 3–15 s clips, the specific thresholds (aesthetic < 4.0, luminance outside [20,140], text area > 30%, motion score 2.0–14.0) are stated without sensitivity analysis, and the claim that the modified PySceneDetect "improves both segmentation accuracy and processing speed" has no supporting numbers. There is also no ablation on the caption-generation design (e.g., how much of the gain in Fig. 9 comes from the pose prior vs. the LLM refinement stage).

strengths: Substantial scale and scope: 21,789 hours of raw in-the-wild video distilled into 2.7M clips / 7,089 hours with per-frame camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions and motion instructions. Table 1 makes a clear and convincing case that this is the largest dynamic video dataset with explicit geometric annotations, well beyond CO3Dv2, RealEstate10K, CamVid-30K, DynPose100K, and the concurrent Sekai (600 hours).

The dataset fills a real and well-motivated gap. The introduction and related work correctly diagnose the split between semantic-only video corpora (Panda70M, OpenVid) and geometry-only datasets (CO3D, RealEstate10K, TartanAir), and SpatialVID's combination of geometry + semantics + motion instructions is genuinely useful for reconstruction, controllable video generation, and world-model research.

The curation pipeline is thorough and thoughtfully designed: motion-first manual screening, a hierarchical quality filter over aesthetics/luminance/OCR/motion (Fig. 5 gives concrete thresholds and illustrative pass/fail examples), and an empirically justified choice of MegaSaM as the pose estimator with a side-by-side trajectory comparison against COLMAP, DROID-SLAM, Fast3R, MonST3R and VGGT (Fig. 6).

The spatial-enhancement of captions is a simple but effective idea: injecting camera pose as a geometric prior into the LLM refinement stage to correct VLM motion-direction errors. Fig. 9 gives a concrete, verifiable example where a 'pan right' description is corrected to 'left'. This is the kind of cross-modal consistency trick that is likely to be reused.

Interpretable, reusable motion representations: the decomposition of relative pose changes into a controlled cinematic vocabulary (dolly in, pan left, truck right) and the introduction of quantitative trajectory metrics (MoveDist, RotAngle, TrajTurns, dynamic ratio) give the community well-defined handles for measuring and conditioning on camera motion.

The quantitative comparison against Panda-70M (Fig. 13) is a reasonable substitute for some of the missing experiments: it shows SpatialVID-HQ has more compact/higher aesthetics and luminance distributions and, importantly, a far richer motion profile (>80% of Panda-70M clips are non-reconstructable due to insufficient motion, vs. a deliberately balanced motion distribution in SpatialVID-HQ).
weaknesses: The paper contains no downstream training or evaluation experiments. There is no demonstration that a model trained or fine-tuned on SpatialVID outperforms one trained on existing data for any task (pose estimation, depth, controllable video generation, navigation). The abstract's claim that the dataset's richness 'directly foster[s] improved model generalization and performance' is therefore asserted rather than evidenced, which is the single largest gap for a dataset paper.

The geometric annotations are pseudo-ground-truth produced by MegaSaM (with UniDepth v2 / Depth Anything v2 depth priors), not verified ground truth. No quantitative accuracy assessment is reported against a dataset with true camera/depth GT (e.g., TartanAir, Sintel, KITTI), so the fidelity of the central spatial signal is unknown. The paper acknowledges MegaSaM's failure modes (moving-object dominance, variable focal length, radial distortion) but never quantifies their incidence on this corpus, and the 'ground-truth camera motion' framing in the abstract overstates what is actually estimated data.

Caption and instruction quality are validated only qualitatively (Figs. 9 and 14). Since the structured captions, scene tags, and motion instructions are generated by Gemini-2.0-flash + Qwen3-30B-A3B, hallucination rates, motion-label accuracy, and instruction correctness should be measured (e.g., via human spot-checks with agreement statistics or automated consistency checks against poses). As written, the semantic layer is unverified.

Annotation-quality control statistics are thin. The manual screening of 33,443 videos is described procedurally, but there is no reporting of inter-annotator agreement, per-reason rejection counts, or the fraction of clips whose pose estimation failed/was flagged as 'Pose Wrong' beyond the aggregate flow in Fig. 2. For a dataset contribution, these numbers matter for assessing reliability.

Dataset availability and licensing are not addressed. There is no statement of where the data/annotations will be hosted, under what license, or how YouTube-sourced content will be redistributed. Reproducibility of a data-centric contribution depends critically on this.

Several pipeline details that determine reproducibility are under-specified: how the relative-pose thresholds for motion-instruction generation were selected, how the adaptive threshold for SAM2 dynamic masking was calibrated, and how the 'motion probability' maps were combined with contours. These are stated at a high level but not with enough precision to reimplement.

Empirical comparison is limited to Panda-70M. Other spatial/semantic datasets (Sekai, CameraBench, VLM4D, Stereo4D) are contrasted only through Table 1 metadata rather than through any shared analysis or benchmark, so the relative value proposition against the closest recent competitors remains partly unsubstantiated.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: large-scale in-the-wild video with explicit spatial annotations (camera pose, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, motion instructions) is scarce, and the reported scale (7,089 hours / 2.7M clips) plus a balanced HQ subset (1,146 hours) is substantial.

The curation pipeline is described in reasonable detail: hierarchical filtering (aesthetics, luminance, OCR, motion), clip segmentation with PySceneDetect modifications, and a documented annotation stack (MegaSaM for pose/depth, SAM2 for dynamic masks, Gemini/Qwen for structured captions).

Serializing camera motion into a controlled cinematographic vocabulary (dolly in, pan left, truck right, etc.) is a sensible, machine-readable representation that could plausibly help controllable video generation and navigation-style training.

The comparison against Panda-70M on aesthetics, luminance, motion, rotation angle, translation distance, and trajectory-turn distributions (Fig. 13) is a reasonable, if limited, piece of evidence that the filtering/sampling procedure shifts the data distribution toward more spatially informative content.
Table 1 provides a useful side-by-side positioning against prior spatial datasets across domain, synthetic/real, dynamic/static, and annotation type.
weaknesses: No downstream experimental validation. For a dataset paper, the central claim in the abstract ('directly foster improved model generalization and performance') is never tested: there is no training or fine-tuning experiment, no baseline comparison, no benchmark showing that models trained on SpatialVID outperform those trained on Panda-70M or other corpora. The manuscript ends with the conclusion; no experiments section exists. This is the single most consequential gap and undermines the paper's stated contributions.

The annotations are pseudo-labels produced by off-the-shelf models (MegaSaM, SAM2, Depth Anything v2/UniDepth v2, Qwen3, Gemini) rather than verified ground truth, yet the abstract describes 'ground-truth camera motion.' No quantitative validation of annotation accuracy is reported (e.g., evaluating MegaSaM-derived poses on Sintel/KITTI/TUM-style sequences, or reporting pose/depth error distributions for the dataset itself). The claimed 'physical plausibility' check via acceleration is a heuristic, not an accuracy measure.

The three 'novel evaluation metrics' (MoveDist, RotAngle, TrajTurns) are simple descriptive statistics of trajectories, not a methodological contribution, and they are not validated as proxies for annotation correctness.

Limited novelty relative to the tooling: the pipeline is largely a composition of existing components (PySceneDetect, PaddleOCR, VMAF, MegaSaM, SAM2, Qwen, Gemini). The paper does not isolate which design choices matter, and no ablations on filter thresholds (aesthetic 4.0, luminance [20,140], OCR 30%) or on the HQ sampling strategy are provided to justify them.

Reproducibility and release are unaddressed: there is no statement about dataset licensing, redistribution rights for YouTube-sourced footage, consent/privacy handling, annotation confidence, or a datasheet. For a web-scraped video dataset this is a material omission.

Comparisons with closely related concurrent work (Sekai, CameraBench, VLM4D, Stereo4D) are relegated to a table and a sentence, without any empirical or annotation-level comparison; the paper claims to 'surpass' them in scale and diversity but provides no head-to-head evidence.

Internal inconsistencies and unclear accounting: Fig. 1 reports 2.7M clips / 720M words, Fig. 3 caption states 3.4M clips in the filtering stage and 2.7M in the base dataset, and Table 1 lists 2.71M clips / 127.60M frames for SpatialVID. The relationship between 21,789 hours of raw footage, ~7M preprocessed clips, and the final 7,089 hours is not transparently reconciled.

No error analysis or failure discussion for the annotation stage on in-the-wild dynamic scenes, where MegaSaM is known to be fragile (large dynamic foregrounds, collinear camera/object motion, variable focal length, radial distortion). The paper acknowledges these limitations in passing but does not quantify how much of the 2.7M clips are affected.

The related work is long and somewhat padded relative to the modest methodological contribution, while the section that would carry the scientific argument (experiments/validation) is absent; the manuscript's substantive content is short.

No human evaluation or VLM-based evaluation of the structured captions is provided, despite the paper's own criticism of VLM captioning quality; the caption 'enhancement' is asserted via length distributions (Fig. 11) and a single qualitative example (Fig. 9), which is insufficient evidence.
